title: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)
summary: Describes Classless Inter-Domain Routing, which allocates IP addresses in flexible blocks instead of fixed classes. This helps conserve the address space and slow the growth of routing tables. It was replaced by RFC 4632.

eli5.summary: Old addresses came in only three sizes, like shoe sizes small, medium, and giant. CIDR lets you buy a size that fits, so less is wasted.

questions: what are the cidr routing rules
subtitle: Handing out IP addresses in flexible, power-of-two blocks so routing tables stop growing out of control.

tldr.problem: The class B address space was running out, routing tables were growing faster than software, hardware and people could manage, and the 32-bit address space would eventually be exhausted.
tldr.mechanism: Allocate blocks of class C network numbers to service providers on bit boundaries, let providers hand out sub-blocks, and route on network and mask pairs using longest match so many routes collapse into one.
tldr.outcome: It was meant as a short-term strategy and does not solve the exhaustion of the 32-bit address space. RFC 1519 was obsoleted by RFC 4632.

today: RFC 1519 is obsoleted by RFC 4632, which now describes CIDR. It obsoleted RFC 1338.

sections.title: The Scaling Problems
sections.content:
The memo names three problems. First, the class B address space was being exhausted: class C, with a maximum of 254 host addresses, is too small for a mid-sized organization, while class B, which allows up to 65534 addresses, is too large. Second, routing tables were growing beyond what current software, hardware and people could manage. Third, the 32-bit IP address space would eventually run out.

The plan targets the first two problems and expects them to become critical within one to three years. It does not try to solve the third. It is a short-term strategy, expected to be viable for at least three years, until a long-term solution is deployed. It does not require already assigned addresses to be reassigned.
sections.eli5: Houses came in only tiny or huge sizes, so mid-sized families took huge ones and wasted space, while the phone book of addresses got too thick to use.

sections.title: Allocation and Aggregation
sections.content:
The plan has two parts: distribute the allocation of address space, and aggregate routing information. The basic idea is to give one or more blocks of class C network numbers to each network service provider. Customers get bitmask-oriented subsets of the provider's space. A transit provider can then advertise one aggregate route instead of one route per customer.

Aggregation works poorly in two cases. Multi-homed organizations must be advertised by each provider. Organizations that change provider without renumbering punch a hole in the old provider's aggregate, so the new provider must advertise a specific route, which wins by longest match. Allocating a contiguous power-of-two block of network numbers lets a site's routes be described by a single network and mask pair.

The RFC recommends that most, if not all, network numbers be distributed through service providers. The benefits it names are that it is easier for a few providers than many clients to get addresses from the central authority, and that allocation becomes scalable and delegatable.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone writing to the city for a house number, the city gives each neighborhood a whole block of numbers, and the neighborhood hands them out. Mail carriers only need to know the neighborhood.

sections.title: Routing Rules
sections.content:
Inter-domain protocols must drop the idea of network class, represent destinations as network and mask pairs, and route on a longest-match basis. Two rules follow.

Rule 1: routing to all destinations is done on longest match only. A destination that is multi-homed relative to a routing domain must be announced explicitly into that domain and cannot be summarized.

Rule 2: a domain that summarizes multiple routes must discard packets that match the summary but none of the explicit routes inside it. This prevents routing loops. One simple implementation is a "sink" route for each aggregation.

Masks must be left contiguous. The route 0.0.0.0 with mask 0.0.0.0 is the default route and MUST be accepted by all implementations, and it should not be advertised unless configuration says to. Aggregation is the responsibility of the domain that was allocated the range, and the RFC recommends preconfiguring the ranges to aggregate rather than learning them dynamically. Older protocols such as EGP2 cannot carry this; the RFC recommends default routes for interoperating with them.
sections.eli5: When two signs match your address, you follow the more specific one. And if a neighborhood sign says "all these streets are ours", the neighborhood must throw away mail for a street that does not exist, not send it back out to loop forever.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC takes a provider "RA" allocated 2048 class C networks starting at 192.24.0.0, described by the aggregate 192.24.0.0 with mask 255.248.0.0. RA serves six clients, for example C1 gets 8 class C networks as 192.24.0.0 mask 255.255.248.0, and C2 gets 16 as 192.24.16.0 mask 255.255.240.0.

Then it adds complications: C4 and C5 are multi-homed through a second provider "RB", and C7 moved from RB to RA while keeping an address from RB's block. By Rule 1, RA advertises its block, C7 and C4 to the backbone "BB". RB advertises its block plus C4 and C5. C5 need not be advertised by RA because longest match at BB selects RB as primary.

The example also shows a side effect: if RA loses C7, BB may forward traffic for C7 to RB's less specific match, where Rule 2 discards it. That is harmless but can confuse someone debugging with traceroute.
sections.eli5: Think of two neighborhoods sharing a big map. One family moved from one to the other but kept its old house number, so the new neighborhood has to put up a special sign for it.

sections.title: Reverse DNS and Class A Extension
sections.content:
Section 6 says the same method could later be applied to the remaining class A space, if the class C space runs out before a long-term solution. This needs routers inside such a class A to use a classless IGP.

Section 7 covers the reverse-lookup IN-ADDR.ARPA zone, which is delegated on octet boundaries only. To work with blocks of class C networks, the RFC recommends allowing delegation of arbitrary octet-oriented pieces. Its example is a provider with 1024 class C networks, 199.0.0 through 199.3.255, which would need only four delegation records instead of 1024.

The Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: The reverse phone book also has to be re-sorted, so a whole neighborhood can be listed in one entry instead of every house on its own line.
